Gates cochaired the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation from 2000 until she stepped down in 2024. She explained that the practice is not about avoiding criticism, but about giving it with honesty, integrity and grace.“Being clear is kind,” French Gates said, “because I’m giving them feedback so they can actually grow and become better.”Gates described her 48-hour feedback mantra as maintaining integrity while keeping the other person’s dignity intact: “gracious, thoughtful, before you go into it.” “I don’t mind conflict,” she told Bloomberg then. “I learned to do it in a way for me that maintained my integrity.”Earlier this month, Melinda French Gates pledged $215 million in new funding for women’s health and called for greater accountability in addressing long-standing gaps in healthcare for women, saying progress should be measured over the next four to five years to determine whether access to treatment is improving. Speaking in a Bloomberg Television interview in London, Gates then said the world remains significantly behind in addressing women's health needs and argued that governments must invest more in research, prevention and data collection."We are way behind on women's health across the world," French Gates said, adding that better evidence is needed to persuade policymakers to prioritise the issue and direct resources where they can have the greatest impact. "Measuring matters," she said. "Let's come back and measure this in four or five years" to assess whether women are better able to access treatments and healthcare support.

Article Title: Phones, laptops and consoles get costlier over memory price hike; OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to gadget buyers: Having DRAM in your devices is 'quite terrible' for the world's limited supply
Article Text:
Phones, laptops and consoles get costlier over memory price hike

Sam Altman says local AI is the wrong answer to the memory shortage

Memory chip shortage pushes up prices of phones, laptops and consoles

Memory makers post record profits as shortage may last till 2030

Buying a new phone, laptop or gaming console has got noticeably costlier this year, and the reason sits inside the device. Memory chips, the DRAM and storage every gadget relies on, have climbed so steeply that brands across categories have passed the cost on to buyers. Now OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, whose AI data centres compete for the same chips, has said that keeping this memory in personal devices is a poor use of a scarce resource.Speaking on Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison, which went live on October 29, Altman pushed back on the idea that running open-source AI models on personal computers would take the load off data centres. "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer," he said, adding that the memory ends up "being used 5% of the time. "Altman's point is about utilisation. Memory in a data centre serves many users through the day, while the RAM in a laptop or phone sits idle for long stretches. "You want maximum utilisation in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment," he said. "Somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."He also said he wants a lot more supply in the market. Altman said OpenAI has built its own chip, is learning to build data centres, and plans to point its robotics programme at making more of them.On memory prices, he admitted the market has not corrected itself, saying "the invisible hand is failing right now."The squeeze is visible in India's smartphone market. OnePlus, Samsung, Oppo and others have revised prices more than once because of rising memory costs, and industry watchers say mobile-grade memory now costs several times what it did a year ago, putting phones under Rs 10,000 at risk.PCs are taking a bigger hit. On October 29, the same day the podcast went live, Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and its shares fell over 20% in extended trading. The company expects the PC market to shrink 12% this year and another 10% in 2027, and does not see memory supply or pricing easing next year. HP has said memory made up about 35% of a laptop's production cost in July, up from 15-18% a quarter earlier.Consoles have not escaped either. Sony has raised PS5 prices twice this year, the Xbox Series X now costs 60% more in the US than it did at its 2020 debut, and Nintendo raised the Switch 2's price in September.Chipmakers are on the other side of this. SK Hynix reported a record quarterly operating profit of 83.3 trillion won (about $62 billion) this week, said more than half its production for 2027 and 2028 is already booked under long-term deals, and warned the shortage could last through 2030. Samsung's preliminary figures put its July-September operating profit at around 107.4 trillion won, its fourth straight record quarter.Altman described the shift on the podcast. Memory makers, he said, once spent $20 billion on capacity to earn $19 billion, and are now each set to make about $100 billion in free cash flow a year. Having nearly gone bankrupt in past cycles by overbuilding, they remain cautious about new factories, which means relief for gadget buyers is unlikely to come quickly.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says keeping memory in personal devices is a poor use of a scarce resource. Altman pushed back on the idea that running open-source AI models on personal computers would take the load off data centres. On memory prices, he admitted the market has not corrected itself, saying "the invisible hand is failing right now"

Article Title: Finnish police launch criminal investigation into Google’s planned $15 billion data centre site
Article Text:
Police investigate drainage and water management

Finnish law enforcement authorities announced on Thursday (October 29) that they have opened a criminal investigation into suspected environmental law violations at the construction site of a planned Google data center in northern Finland. According to news agency Reuters, the site is a key component of Alphabet-owned Google’s massive $15 billion artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure plan unveiled last month – an initiative the US tech giant characterised as its single largest investment in Europe.According to authorities, Google subsidiary Tuike Finland initiated forest clearing and land drainage operations near the town of Muhos before completing the mandatory environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law. A Google spokesperson stated that the firm will cooperate fully with law enforcement and will remain focused on upholding compliance across all of its properties.The investigation centers on whether earthworks and water control methods at the development breached national water regulations.“We are investigating whether the company's operations have breached the water act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen was quoted as saying.Pakanen noted that if the company is found guilty, the case could result in a corporate fine, though he declined to say whether individual employees or executives could become targets of the inquiry.In an official statement, police reported that preliminary findings revealed ambiguities and shortcomings regarding water management and drainage on the Tuike property. Authorities plan to release an update in December, but indicated the full investigation will extend into 2027.The police probe follows regulatory intervention earlier in the month. On October 6, Finland's Supervisory Agency (LVV), which is the administrative body responsible for overseeing environmental permits and assessments, ordered Google to immediately suspend all preparatory work that alters the natural environment at the Muhos plot and an additional separate location.Pakanen noted that determining whether permits will be granted to restart work remains strictly the jurisdiction of the LVV. An LVV spokesperson stated it is currently unclear how long it will take to determine whether those permits will be issued.“We've partnered closely with the government and communities in Finland on infrastructure for over a decade, and are actively responding to enquiries from LVV and other authorities,” Google's spokesperson said.Meanwhile, Finland has established itself as one of Europe’s leading hubs for tech infrastructure, thanks to its cold northern climate, low-carbon power grid, and active government backing for AI initiatives. Despite covering an area comparable to Germany, Finland is home to fewer than 6 million people and has historically encountered less local pushback against large-scale computing facilities than regions like the United States.Google’s broader infrastructure program in the country is planned to encompass data centers, power grid upgrades, and clean energy and battery storage systems designed to handle computing loads for core products, including Gemini, Search, Google Maps and YouTube.However, the rapid expansion is placing new demands on national infrastructure. State grid operator Fingrid has projected that domestic electricity consumption could jump by up to 40% in the coming years if all contracted data center grid connections move forward.
Article Summary: Finnish authorities have opened a criminal investigation into suspected environmental law violations at the construction site of a Google data center. The investigation centers on whether earthworks and water control methods at the development breached national water regulations. The site is a key component of Alphabet-owned Google’s massive $15 billion artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure plan unveiled last month.

American intelligence agencies have concluded that a Chinese businesswoman with a close relationship to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was passing information to Beijing, according to a New York Times report. The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company already under US scrutiny for allegedly steering advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to act, the report says. Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, the warning US agencies sometimes give Americans targeted by foreign spies. Surveillance of Alice Huang is still ongoing, and companies linked to her kept buying Nvidia chips this year.China has rejected the allegation. Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, accused the US of running a campaign of baseless smears against Beijing.Nvidia played it down. Spokesperson John Rizzo said Huang's meetings with her were neither unusual nor unexpected, adding that "Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."He said customers like Megaspeed get routine business information, not trade secrets, and nothing relevant to national security. Megaspeed said it has hired outside counsel for an internal probe and will cooperate with the US government.Citing people briefed on the matter, NYT reports that US agencies were electronically monitoring Alice Huang when they found she was in contact with an American citizen. A process known as unmasking later identified that person as the Nvidia chief.When Trump was first briefed, officials did not think Jensen Huang knew what she was doing. Some senior administration officials now doubt he could have stayed in the dark. The two were photographed at a Taipei bar in June 2024, sharing whiskey with other AI executives after a trade show. They were spotted again leaving a business dinner in the city in May 2025.Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment with Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, NYT reports, citing ImportGenius trade records. The firm buys chips, builds data centres in Southeast Asia and rents the computing power to Chinese companies, with Alibaba as its main client.US investigators suspect some of those chips are slipping into China illegally. The Commerce Department began looking into Megaspeed in late 2024, after an official visiting its Malaysian data centre found the Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes. That case has since moved to the Justice Department.The findings surface weeks before Trump's visit to China next month, where chip exports are likely to be on the agenda. Jensen Huang has spent Trump's second term lobbying to ease curbs on Nvidia sales to China, and he sat at the head table when Xi Jinping attended a White House state dinner last month.
Article Summary: US surveillance of a Megaspeed executive led officials straight to Jensen Huang.Megaspeed bought $4.8 billion of Nvidia-powered gear in under two years. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to act.

Article Title: US Homeland Security investigates potential breach after data of 40,000 employees leaked online; records include surveillance and undercover job details
Article Text:

US Homeland Security is investigating a potential breach of employee data. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the response follows an announcement by Distributed Denial of Secrets that it had released records on more than 40,000 Department of Homeland Security employees. The material includes contact information and details identifying personnel assigned to surveillance, special operations, and undercover work.DHS said it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The department said it was working to protect employees and would provide further information when available. Reuters could not immediately authenticate the entire collection, although it independently confirmed some employees’ details. The source of the data and how it was obtained remain unverified.The records include names, phone numbers, and email addresses of employees across DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.Job titles and email group memberships also identify assignments involving computer forensics, surveillance, special operations, human intelligence and undercover work, Reuters reported.Some entries match information employees have published on LinkedIn. Others reveal nonpublic details about internal organisation charts or previously undisclosed programs and operations.The report matched information about six employees against credit bureau records and previously breached data held by intelligence platform District 4 Labs. It also called three employees and confirmed their phone numbers and other details. One said the call was their first notification of a possible breach.Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the records came from an entity calling itself Department of Peace. The entity did not immediately respond to the publication’s request for comment. In a statement accompanying the release, it argued that DHS employeesIn March, the Department of Peace claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and publishing documents about contracts with outside vendors. Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said a search tool helps journalists examine the records, prepare public records requests, and support congressional oversight.Best’s statement said the Department of Peace obtained the employee data through the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Such services allow staff to access workplace applications through a central login. The publication could not immediately corroborate that account. Okta rejected the suggestion that its systems had been breached.the company said in response to the publication.The disclosure comes after other reported government data security incidents. In September, hacking group ShinyHunters said it had stolen information about FBI employees, including sensitive job information and medical records. Separately, the Defence Department faced a class action lawsuit after a breach exposed the data of millions of current and former military personnel.
Article Summary: US Homeland Security is investigating a potential breach of employee data. Records include names, phone numbers, and email addresses of employees across DHS agencies. Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the records came from an entity calling itself Department of Peace. Okta disputes claims that its systems were compromised.

Trump Accounts launched on July 4

Michael Dell has hailed the Trump Accounts program as a growing national movement. Dell CEO took to social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) to share the details of fresh contributions from Silicon Valley and beyond. In a reaction pots, Dell wrote, “This is how a moment becomes a movement.” For those unaware, this initiative is designed to give every American child under 18 a stake in the stock market. It has already opened 9 million accounts and is on track to auto-create accounts for all 70 million children using Social Security data.Dell's post highlighted a growing list of high-profile donors stepping up to fund Trump Accounts, the tax-deferred investment savings program for American children under 18. Among the names: Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, who is contributing $250 each to Trump Accounts for more than 140,000 children in Indiana, and hedge fund manager Ray Dalio and his wife Barbara, who are extending similar $250 contributions to children across Connecticut.The biggest single commitment by dollar value came from SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell, who — along with her husband, Robert — is donating one share of SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children, a gift Dell's post pegs at roughly $325 million.The donation is specifically targeted at children between the ages of 11 and 17 in lower-income communities, continuing a pattern Shotwell set earlier this year when she first announced the gift shortly after SpaceX's record-breaking public listing.Dell used the post to personally thank Gerstner for organizing the broader donor push through Invest America, crediting him for turning the concept into reality, and thanked every donor who has stepped up to participate.Trump Accounts launched on July 4, offering a one-time $1,000 contribution from the US Treasury for every child born between 2025 and 2028, with the accounts open more broadly to all American children under 18. According to Gerstner, who has been central to building out the program's donor infrastructure, roughly 9 million accounts are currently open, with plans in motion to automatically create accounts for all 70 million children under 18 nationwide using Social Security data within the coming month.Michael and Susan Dell have themselves been among the largest backers of the initiative, having pledged a combined $6.25 billion earlier this year to fund $250 contributions for children in lower- and middle-income ZIP codes. Beyond individual philanthropy, Gerstner noted that employers are increasingly layering their own contributions on top of the government's, treating it as an extension of existing 401(k)-style benefits.
Article Summary: Trump Accounts launched on July 4, offering a one-time $1,000 contribution from the US Treasury for every child born between 2025 and 2028. The initiative is designed to give every American child under 18 a stake in the stock market. It has already opened 9 million accounts and is on track to auto-create accounts for all 70 million children using Social Security data.
